title: Addiction: Reducing Addiction
welcome_lead: Drugs, behavioural interventions and public health campaigns — toolkits for change.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology addiction reduction: drug therapy, behavioural interventions, public health.

concepts.def: Synthetic opioid replacement therapy for heroin addiction.
Gum, patches, vapes — replace nicotine, remove tobacco harms.
Pairing addictive behaviour with unpleasant stimulus.
Aversion in imagination — vivid mental punishment.
Client-centred talk eliciting reasons for change.

walkthroughs.body_html: Methadone — full agonist replacing heroin; reduces cravings and crime. NRT doubles long-term quit rates compared to placebo (Stead 2012). Disulfiram makes alcohol unpleasant by blocking acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors to reduce reward.

Aversion therapy pairs the addictive cue with electric shock, nausea-inducing drug or unpleasant imagery. Covert sensitisation (Cautela 1967) is imagined version — patient imagines smoking then vomiting. Evidence is mixed; relapse high without follow-up.

UK Change4Life and Australian graphic cigarette warnings target attitudes and perceived risk. Most campaigns use fear appeals: moderate fear with self-efficacy works best. Wakefield et al. (2010): mass campaigns reduce smoking prevalence by 1-2% annually.
